Generated from `packages/seyd-qos/src/lib.rs`. A profile is a *ceiling*: the closed-loop
controller moves the bitrate request and the FEC rates inside it, never above it. The
robot picks a profile (`qos_profile` in `seydd.toml`, `seyd_set_qos_profile`,
`Agent.set_qos_profile`) and a driver may ask for another (`SeydSession.setQos`).
Degrade resolution first and frame rate last: for a remote pilot, the interval between
frames is latency, not quality.

## Targets the publisher must honour (sent as `video-config`)

| Field | `latency` | `balanced` | `quality` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_bitrate_kbps` | `1500` | `3000` | `6000` | The ceiling on the publisher's video bitrate; the closed-loop controller moves the actual request between 25 % of this and this. |
| `latency_budget_ms` | `100` | `100` | `200` | How much end-to-end delay the profile is prepared to spend, told to the publisher so it can size its own buffers (VBV, lookahead). |
| `max_gop_ms` | `10000` | `10000` | `4000` | The longest the publisher may go without a full recovery point — an IDR, or a completed intra-refresh sweep. |
| `prefer_intra_refresh` | `true` | `true` | `true` | Ask the publisher to refresh the picture gradually — a strip of intra-coded blocks per frame sweeping the picture within `max_gop_ms` — rather than with periodic IDRs, where its encoder can (x264, NVENC, Jetson; not the ONVIF cameras surveyed). |

## Seyd's own transport policy

| Field | `latency` | `balanced` | `quality` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fec_delta_pct` | `25` | `15` | `8` | Reed-Solomon parity added to a delta frame's block, as a percentage of its data chunks, on a clean link; the controller raises it under loss. |
| `fec_key_pct` | `50` | `30` | `15` | Parity for keyframes, which are larger and cost a GOP if torn. |
| `backlog_drop_frames` | `1` | `2` | `3` | Drop a delta frame if the send backlog exceeds this many frame-times. |
| `recovery_grace_ms` | `700` | `900` | `1400` | How long the sender waits for a recovery point after asking for one before it resumes sending delta frames regardless. |

## Pilot policy

| Field | `latency` | `balanced` | `quality` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pilot_deadline_delta_ms` | `20` | `30` | `50` | How long the pilot waits for a delta frame's missing chunks before closing it out. |
| `pilot_deadline_key_ms` | `40` | `60` | `100` | The same wait for a keyframe. |
| `pilot_presentation_delay_ms` | `50` | `100` | `150` | How long the pilot holds a decoded frame past its capture slot before painting it (ADR 0005). |
| `on_loss` | `Continue` | `Continue` | `FreezeUntilIdr` | What the pilot does when a frame cannot be repaired: keep decoding (`continue`, and ask for a recovery point) or freeze until the next IDR. |

## Field notes

### `name`

The profile's name: `latency`, `balanced` or `quality`.

### `max_bitrate_kbps`

The ceiling on the publisher's video bitrate; the closed-loop controller moves the actual request between 25 % of this and this.

### `latency_budget_ms`

How much end-to-end delay the profile is prepared to spend, told to the publisher so it can size its own buffers (VBV, lookahead).

### `max_gop_ms`

The longest the publisher may go without a full recovery point — an IDR, or a completed intra-refresh sweep. A *ceiling*, and a safety net: Seyd asks for recovery points when it needs them (`recovery-request`), so the periodic one only has to catch a publisher that ignores it (ADR 0009). It is long on purpose: a periodic IDR is several times a delta frame, and measured on the demo camera it arrived ~22 ms late and made every GOP's first two intervals 60 ms then 18 ms; at 10 s GOPs arrival judder fell from 3.7 to 0.9 ms mean and the stream lost 43 % of its bitrate, the IDRs' share. A joining pilot never waits for it: the agent asks for an IDR on `hello`.

### `prefer_intra_refresh`

Ask the publisher to refresh the picture gradually — a strip of intra-coded blocks per frame sweeping the picture within `max_gop_ms` — rather than with periodic IDRs, where its encoder can (x264, NVENC, Jetson; not the ONVIF cameras surveyed). Removes the keyframe burst entirely; measured on the sim through a shaped link as g2g p95 148 → 48 ms (docs/latency-sources.md §11).

### `fec_delta_pct`

Reed-Solomon parity added to a delta frame's block, as a percentage of its data chunks, on a clean link; the controller raises it under loss.

### `fec_key_pct`

Parity for keyframes, which are larger and cost a GOP if torn.

### `backlog_drop_frames`

Drop a delta frame if the send backlog exceeds this many frame-times.

### `pilot_deadline_delta_ms`

How long the pilot waits for a delta frame's missing chunks before closing it out.

### `pilot_deadline_key_ms`

The same wait for a keyframe.

### `pilot_presentation_delay_ms`

How long the pilot holds a decoded frame past its capture slot before painting it (ADR 0005). This is the profile's judder-versus-latency call: a keyframe is ~8x a delta frame and is produced in one frame slot, so without a budget here the picture hitches once per GOP. It is a bound, not an average — a frame never waits longer than this past its own arrival — so it is the latency the profile is prepared to spend. 0 disables pacing and restores decode-on-arrival.

### `recovery_grace_ms`

How long the sender waits for a recovery point after asking for one before it resumes sending delta frames regardless.  A publisher that recovers with intra-refresh or an LTR reference never produces a keyframe, so waiting for one latches the stream silent forever. Roughly one refresh cycle: long enough that a real keyframe arrives first when the publisher sends IDRs, short enough that a stall is not visible as a freeze.

### `on_loss`

What the pilot does when a frame cannot be repaired: keep decoding (`continue`, and ask for a recovery point) or freeze until the next IDR.
